strengths: Novel test-time optimization approach that produces localized embeddings without any finetuning of the backbone, making it broadly applicable as a drop-in replacement across diverse downstream applications (classification, captioning, diffusion).

Clever gradient decomposition trick that exploits the frozen backbone to significantly reduce the cost of the iterative explainability-map-based optimization, with clear runtime benefits demonstrated as the number of masks grows.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many datasets and tasks (PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, MSCOCO, OpenImagesV7) and multiple backbone sizes, generally outperforming strong recent baselines including AlphaCLIP without requiring millions of mask-text annotations.

Good ablations covering mask quality/robustness (boxes, SAM-derived masks, erosion/dilation), choice of explainability method (LeGrad vs GradCAM/CheferCAM), and computational efficiency of gradient decomposition.

Method is conceptually simple, model-agnostic, and demonstrated to generalize across CLIP variants and even to entirely different downstream modules (LLM captioner, diffusion model) without retraining those modules.
Reasonably thorough related work discussion and an honest limitations section acknowledging dependence on explainability method quality and low-resolution backbone constraints.
weaknesses: Per-mask, per-image test-time optimization (10 gradient descent iterations) could be substantially slower than single-forward-pass alternatives (Crop, Masked Crop, AlphaCLIP) for large-scale deployment; despite the gradient decomposition speedup, an absolute wall-clock/throughput comparison against baselines is missing, only relative decomposition-vs-vanilla timings are shown.

The comparison table for referring expressions mixes reported numbers from differing evaluation protocols (proposal-based vs GT-mask-based) with reproduced numbers, which complicates fair, direct comparison to prior SOTA methods (CPT, ReCLIP, RedCircle, FGVP, AlphaCLIP) despite the paper's caveats.

The regularization loss hyperparameter α is manually set per-dataset (0 vs 5) rather than learned or validated systematically, raising concerns about tuning overhead and generalizability to new tasks/datasets.

Quantitative evaluation of localized captioning and diffusion applications is limited: captioning is evaluated only via a somewhat indirect proxy metric (cosine similarity matching to referring expressions) on a single adapted dataset, and diffusion results are entirely qualitative with no quantitative metrics (e.g., CLIP-score, FID, or human evaluation).

No ablation on the number of optimization steps K or convergence behavior/sensitivity in the main text (only briefly touched via appendix runtime figure), leaving open whether 10 steps is a robustly chosen default across tasks and backbones.

Reliance on LeGrad as the explainability method is shown to be important (Table 6 shows large gaps versus GradCAM/CheferCAM), suggesting the method's effectiveness may be tightly coupled to specific explainability techniques for ViTs, potentially limiting generality to non-ViT or non-CLIP-style architectures.

Some numerical/typographical errors and unclear table entries in the paper (e.g., PascalVOC Acc@5 value of 8.9 for MaskInversion in Table 2, apparent typo) reduce polish and could indicate insufficiently careful proofreading of results.

strengths: Introduces a novel test-time optimization approach (MaskInversion) for generating localized embeddings from frozen vision-language foundation models without any fine-tuning, using explainability maps as supervision signal — this is a clean and elegant reuse of explainability methods as an optimization objective rather than just a diagnostic tool.

Broad demonstrated applicability: the same learned token acts as a drop-in replacement for the CLS token across three very different downstream pipelines (zero-shot region classification, localized captioning via CLIPCap, and localized image variation via a diffusion model) without retraining any of those downstream models.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across many datasets (PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, MSCOCO, OpenImagesV7) and multiple CLIP backbone sizes, with consistent improvements over reproduced baselines (Crop, Masked Crop, RedCircle, FGVP, AlphaCLIP, RIS), and performance that scales favorably with backbone size.

The gradient decomposition trick is a useful, well-motivated efficiency contribution that meaningfully reduces runtime when processing multiple masks per image, supported by a reasonably thorough runtime ablation.

Includes informative ablations on mask quality (box vs. mask vs. SAM-refined box), sensitivity to the choice of explainability method, and the effect of the regularization loss, which help characterize the method's robustness and design choices.
Avoids the need for large-scale mask-text annotation (unlike AlphaCLIP), which is a practical advantage, and the method is backbone-agnostic in principle.
weaknesses: The explainability-method ablation (Table 6) reveals a very large performance gap between LeGrad (85.4) and other explainability methods such as GradCAM (34.6) or CheferCAM (12.6), suggesting the method is considerably less 'general' than claimed and is in practice tightly coupled to one specific explainability technique; this undercuts the generality claim made in the abstract/intro.

No end-to-end latency/wall-clock comparison against baselines (e.g., AlphaCLIP, FGVP, RedCircle) is provided; the paper only reports relative speedups from gradient decomposition versus its own vanilla variant, leaving open how practical MaskInversion is compared to single-forward-pass alternatives, especially given it requires K iterative gradient steps per mask at test time.

The localized diffusion application (Section 4.4) is evaluated only qualitatively; no quantitative metrics (e.g., CLIP-score alignment, FID, or human preference) are reported to substantiate the claimed quality of localized image generation.

The localized captioning evaluation relies on an indirect, automatic proxy metric (cosine similarity between generated caption and the closest ground-truth referring expression), which may not reliably reflect actual caption quality/fluency; no human evaluation or standard captioning metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, etc.) are included.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different backbone combinations across baseline methods (e.g., RN50x16+ViT-B/32 vs. ViT-B/16), and results are split between 'reported' and 'reproduced' numbers under different evaluation protocols, which complicates direct, fair comparison despite the authors' caveats.
Limited justification/ablation for the choice of K=10 optimization steps and the AdamW hyperparameters; a quality-vs-compute tradeoff curve as a function of K would strengthen the efficiency claims.

The paper has some clarity/writing issues (e.g., garbled sentences such as 'MaskInversion also significantly AlphaCLIP' and 'performance scall-well'), which slightly detract from readability and suggest the draft would benefit from further proofreading.

strengths: Introduces a novel test-time optimization approach that derives localized region embeddings from frozen vision-language foundation models by matching explainability maps to query masks, avoiding any fine-tuning of the backbone.

Proposes a mathematically well-justified gradient decomposition strategy that substantially reduces computational cost when handling multiple masks per image, with clear derivation and supporting runtime experiments.

Extensive evaluation across a diverse set of downstream tasks (referring expression retrieval, zero-shot class retrieval, localized captioning, localized diffusion) and datasets (PascalVOC, PascalContext, MSCOCO, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, PhraseCut, OpenImagesV7), showing consistent improvements over multiple baselines.
Demonstrates that the method outperforms AlphaCLIP despite AlphaCLIP being fine-tuned on millions of mask-text pairs, highlighting the value of not needing backbone adaptation.

Thorough set of ablations covering mask quality/robustness, regularization weight alpha, choice of explainability method, number of optimization iterations, and runtime scaling with resolution/number of masks.
Good scalability behavior with backbone size (ViT-B/32 to ViT-H/14), with performance improving consistently as model capacity increases.
Qualitative results (captioning, diffusion generation, multi-object masks) provide intuitive support for the claims and illustrate practical applicability as a drop-in embedding replacement.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols across baselines are inconsistent (marked by ‡ vs * reproduced results with different region-proposal or ground-truth mask settings), which complicates direct fair comparison with prior state-of-the-art methods like CPT, ReCLIP, RedCircle, and FGVP.

The method's effectiveness is shown to be highly sensitive to the choice of explainability method (Table 8, LeGrad vs GradCAM/CheferCAM shows huge gaps), suggesting fragility and limiting generality across different backbones/explainability techniques not yet well-supported by LeGrad.

Per-mask, per-image test-time optimization (10 gradient steps per mask) introduces non-trivial inference-time cost compared to single-forward-pass baselines (e.g., simple Masked Crop, which is already a surprisingly strong baseline), and the practical latency/throughput trade-off in realistic deployment scenarios (e.g., many objects per image, video, real-time use) is not thoroughly analyzed.

The convergence analysis shows the Dice loss keeps decreasing well beyond K=10 while downstream accuracy plateaus, suggesting a potential loose coupling between the explainability-matching objective and actual semantic embedding quality that is not deeply investigated.
No reported variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance across runs, despite the method's stochastic optimization procedure with random initialization/token learning.

Localized captioning and multi-object handling evaluations rely substantially on qualitative examples with limited quantitative rigor (e.g., the multi-object claims are entirely qualitative), reducing confidence in generalizability of these claims.

The paper does not clearly quantify or compare end-to-end wall-clock/throughput overhead of MaskInversion relative to simpler competitive baselines (e.g., Masked Crop, AlphaCLIP single pass) in the main results tables, making it harder to judge the practical cost-benefit trade-off of the approach.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: using explainability maps (LeGrad) as an optimization signal to derive a localized, context-aware embedding for a query region at test time, without finetuning the backbone. This differs meaningfully from prior visual-prompting (crop/blur/circle) and finetuning-based (AlphaCLIP, CPT) approaches.

Method is architecture-agnostic and works as a drop-in replacement for the [CLS] token, demonstrated across four different CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32 to ViT-H/14) with consistent performance gains that scale with model size.

Broad and consistent empirical validation across multiple, meaningfully different downstream tasks: referring expression retrieval (PhraseCut, RefCOCO, RefCOCO+), open-vocabulary class retrieval (PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, OpenImagesV7), localized captioning, and localized image generation.

Outperforms strong recent baselines, including AlphaCLIP, despite AlphaCLIP being finetuned on millions of mask-text annotations, and outperforms several training-free aggregation methods (MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, SCLIP), with the performance gap widening for larger backbones.

Thoughtful engineering contribution: the gradient decomposition trick for reusing the Jacobian across iterations and masks is mathematically justified (formal derivation in appendix) and empirically shown to reduce runtime for multi-mask images.

Thorough ablation suite: mask-quality robustness (erosion/dilation/box/SAM-derived masks), sensitivity to the regularization hyperparameter α, choice of explainability method, number of optimization iterations/convergence behavior, and runtime scaling with resolution.

Good qualitative results (multi-object handling, localized diffusion, localized captioning) that support the quantitative claims and provide interpretability via explainability-map visualizations across optimization steps.
weaknesses: The method's effectiveness is closely tied to the choice of explainability method — the ablation shows a huge performance gap between LeGrad (85.4%) and alternatives like GradCAM (34.6%) or CheferCAM (12.6%), suggesting the approach is not as backbone/method-agnostic as claimed and raising concerns about robustness/generality if LeGrad is unavailable or performs poorly on other architectures.

Evaluation for localized captioning relies on a proxy metric (cosine similarity ranking against ground-truth referring expressions) rather than standard captioning metrics (CIDEr/BLEU/METEOR) or human evaluation, making it harder to judge true caption quality.

The localized diffusion application is only evaluated qualitatively; no quantitative metrics (e.g., CLIP-score, FID, or user study) are provided to substantiate claims about the fidelity/consistency of generated images relative to the query mask.

Table 1 combines results reported in prior papers (different eval protocols with region proposals and IoU>0.5 hit criterion) with the authors' own reproductions under a different ground-truth-mask setting, which, despite disclaimers, makes some baseline comparisons not fully apples-to-apples and could be presented more cleanly.

Test-time optimization (10 gradient steps per mask) adds inference-time overhead compared to single-forward-pass baselines (Crop, Masked Crop, training-free aggregation methods); although gradient decomposition mitigates this for many masks, for single-mask or few-mask use cases the method is likely slower than simpler alternatives, and this trade-off could be more prominently discussed in the main text.

Gains over AlphaCLIP on the large-vocabulary OpenImagesV7 benchmark (which is closer to AlphaCLIP's training distribution) are comparatively modest, suggesting the advantage may be less pronounced in some open-vocabulary, large-scale settings.

No quantitative failure-case analysis (e.g., performance breakdown by mask size, occlusion level, or object density) despite the multi-object and small-object limitations being acknowledged only qualitatively/textually.
